newsitem.title: CANADA: Nickel market ignores Inco lockout for now.
newsitem.headline: Nickel market ignores Inco lockout for now.

text.p: The world nickel market has turned a blind eye to a week-long labor dispute that has halted production at Inco Ltd's Manitoba facility.
But if the dispute drags on long enough, nickel prices will start to rise, analysts and industry official said.
Inco shut down the plant a week ago, locking out almost 1,400 members of the United Steelworkers after they voted to reject the company's final contract offer.
The Thompson facility produces about 100 million pounds of nickel a year, or about 20 percent of Inco's total output.
The labor dispute has so far had little impact on nickel prices, despite a delicate balance in world supply and demand that has kept the commodity price in check for months.
"Nickel is just holding in there," Patricia Mohr, economist for Bank of Nova Scotia, said in an interview.
"The base metal markets are very quiet. I think they're waiting for industrial demand to pick up."
A surplus of stainless steel, which absorbs about two-thirds of the world nickel supply, has kept a rise in the nickel price at bay, she said.
But the nickel price will eventually react, she added.
The cash price for nickel on the London Metal Exchange has fallen steadily since the lockout began.
With no production from Inco's Thompson facility, and output cut by a third at Inco's Indonesia facility becaushe company said.
Last week, a government conciliator gave up on brokering an agreement because the sides were too far apart. The parties have not met since talks broke down a week ago.
